grammarNotes: Irish Overseer Influence (cy- / ky- sound): Words starting with c or k before certain vowels often take a cy- or ky- sound (e.g., car → cyar, can't → cy'an, cart → cyart, look here → look-kyea).
Alveolar Stops (th → d or t): The th sound in Standard English is consistently replaced with d or t (e.g., the → deh / de, them → dem, that → dat, thing → ting, Thursday → Taws-Deh).
Vowel Shifts & Pronunciations (down → dung): Words ending in standard -own often take a -ung sound (e.g., down → dung).

West African Languages (Twi, Yoruba, Igbo, Kongo, Tshiluba, Fon): Heavy influence on vocabulary (Anansi, kalaloo, jumbie, nyam, gongolo) and semantic calques/loan-translations (door mout, sweet eye, strong eye, foot meaning entire leg).

Danish Rule Influences: Vestiges of Danish colonial history preserved in everyday dialect (gade = street from Danish gade; potekari = pharmacy from Danish apotek; frickadella = meatballs from frikadeller; skaal = drinking toast from skål; pascalam = Easter party from Fastelavn).
Negerhollands (Dutch Creole): Substrate roots found in terms like pistarckle, jumbie, fungee, and zamba.
Spanish & Puerto Rican Cross-Pollination: Terms absorbed from Spanish-speaking neighbors (bacalao, chabos, adobo, coki, crapo, fraco, barato → brata).
Acts as the article "the" ("deh dawg" = "the dog").
Doubled ("deh deh") to indicate location "there" ("Deh dawg dem deh deh" = "The dogs are there").
In negative location sentences, one deh is dropped ("Me'en deh yah" = "I'm not here").

Aspect & Habitual Marker ("Does"): Used to mark habitual action, present continuous, or past habitual actions depending on context ("We does sing as we walk" = "We sang as we walked" / "We usually sing when we walk").
Reduplication for Emphasis: Doubling words to heighten intensity ("true true" = genuinely true; "far far" = extremely distant; "big big" = overly boastful; "talk talk" = constant gossip).
Informal Register: Crucian has no formal vs. informal register distinction; the dialect as a whole is expressive and personal.

proverbs.translation: A crab never forgets its hole.
proverbs.meaning: There is no place like home; also, people will always reveal their true nature/origins.

proverbs.translation: An eyeful is not a bellyful.
proverbs.meaning: Looking at something is not the same as having it; solving one small issue doesn't solve all problems.

proverbs.text: Ah have a lil rat in eb'ry hole.
proverbs.translation: I have a little rat in every hole.
proverbs.meaning: I have connections and friends in all the right places.

proverbs.text: All wood is wood, bu' mampoo ain' mahogany.
proverbs.translation: All wood is wood, but softwood (mampoo) isn't mahogany.
proverbs.meaning: Don't judge by superficial appearances; true value and quality matter.

proverbs.text: Dag ga' four foot but 'e caan tek four road.
proverbs.translation: A dog has four feet, but it can't take four roads.
proverbs.meaning: One person cannot be in multiple places at once or pursue conflicting paths simultaneously.

proverbs.text: Do for do ain' no obeah.
proverbs.translation: Doing in return isn't witchcraft.
proverbs.meaning: Tit-for-tat or returning a favor/action is fair play, not malice or bad magic.
A very long time.
Doorway or entrance (calque from West African Yoruba iloro enu / Igbo onu uzo).

proverbs.text: Every skin teeth ain' a grin.
proverbs.translation: Every smile isn't a genuine grin.
proverbs.meaning: Not everyone who smiles in your face is your friend; beware of fake friendliness.

proverbs.text: Ev'ry donkey bray in 'e own pasture.
proverbs.translation: Every donkey brays in its own pasture.
proverbs.meaning: Everyone has their own unique tastes, preferences, and personal style.

proverbs.text: Ev'ry house ga' a dutty corner.
proverbs.translation: Every house has a dirty corner.
proverbs.meaning: Everyone has a secret flaw, personal issue, or skeleton in their closet.

proverbs.text: Ev'ry tub mus' sit on its own bottom.
proverbs.translation: Every tub must sit on its own bottom.
proverbs.meaning: Practice self-reliance, independence, and personal responsibility.

proverbs.text: Head no mek fo' hat alone!
proverbs.translation: Your head wasn't made just to wear a hat!
proverbs.meaning: Use your brain and think clearly before acting.

proverbs.text: Knead the flour, now cut the bread.
proverbs.translation: Knead the flour, now cut the bread.
proverbs.meaning: Action time has arrived; put your plans into practice.

proverbs.text: Monkey know wha' tree to clime.
proverbs.translation: A monkey knows which tree to climb.
proverbs.meaning: People know who they can fool or push around, and who they shouldn't mess with.

proverbs.translation: Never grease a fat pig.
proverbs.meaning: Don't waste gifts or favors on people who already have more than enough.

proverbs.text: New broom sweep clean, Old broom know de corners.
proverbs.translation: A new broom sweeps clean, but an old broom knows the corners.
proverbs.meaning: New people bring fresh energy, but experienced people understand how things work.

proverbs.translation: An old chicken makes good soup.
proverbs.meaning: Older, experienced people hold great value, wisdom, and resourcefulness.

proverbs.translation: One bite can't finish a mango.
proverbs.meaning: Complex or large tasks require patience, time, and step-by-step effort.

proverbs.translation: One single penny cannot jingle by itself.
proverbs.meaning: It takes two to tango; conflict or cooperation requires two participating parties.
Think carefully before taking action (calque, compare Yoruba).

proverbs.translation: Time is longer than string/twine.
proverbs.meaning: Patience is necessary; outcomes and consequences take time, but time outlasts everything.
Genuinely true, authentic (reduplication).

proverbs.text: Wha' gone bad in de mornin' caan' come good in de evening.
proverbs.translation: What goes wrong in the morning won't fix itself by evening.
proverbs.meaning: Issues that start off poorly will not rectify themselves without deliberate effort.

proverbs.text: Wha' sweet 'e mout' does sour 'e bottom.
proverbs.translation: What tastes sweet in the mouth sours the bottom.
proverbs.meaning: Short-term, foolish pleasures often lead to long-term pain.

proverbs.text: What yoh do in de dark does come to light.
proverbs.translation: What you do in the dark comes to light.
proverbs.meaning: Secrets and hidden misdeeds will eventually be exposed.

proverbs.text: When de wind blow foul, batty does show.
proverbs.translation: When the wind blows hard, the chicken's rear end shows.
proverbs.meaning: When unexpected hardship or pressure occurs, a person's true character and hidden flaws are revealed.

proverbs.text: Ah gon..." (e.g., "Ah gon buss yo lip" / "Ah gon pong yo behind")
proverbs.translation: I am going to... (hit/punish you).
proverbs.meaning: Standard opening phrase of a stern warning or threat of physical discipline.

proverbs.text: After sweet meat come sour sauce.
proverbs.translation: After sweet meat comes sour sauce.
proverbs.meaning: Reckless living or indulgence carries a steep price eventually.

proverbs.text: All fish does bite, but shark does get de blame.
proverbs.translation: All fish bite, but the shark gets the blame.
proverbs.meaning: People with bad reputations are automatically blamed whenever trouble occurs.
Sucking teeth to express annoyance, anger, or contempt (African cultural origin).

proverbs.translation: A dog doesn't need a bone only once.
proverbs.meaning: Help others when they ask a favor; you will likely need assistance from them in the future.
To soil or make dirty (compare Twi dote).
A jinx; a person who utters bad predictions that end up coming true.

proverbs.text: If you cyan dance, don't blame de floor!
proverbs.translation: If you can't dance, don't blame the dance floor!
proverbs.meaning: Accept responsibility for your own shortcomings instead of making excuses.

proverbs.text: If you dig up old grave, do it smell stink?
proverbs.translation: If you dig up an old grave, does it smell foul?
proverbs.meaning: Don't reopen old arguments or dwell on past grievances.

proverbs.text: If yo'u no hear 'e bell, yo'll live and hear 'e big bell.
proverbs.translation: If you don't hear the small bell, you'll live to hear the big bell.
proverbs.meaning: Ignore minor warnings now, and you will face severe consequences later.

proverbs.text: Jackass ga' no business in hoss race.
proverbs.translation: A donkey has no business in a horse race.
proverbs.meaning: Stay in your lane; do not interfere in matters beyond your standing.

proverbs.translation: The kettle is calling the bottom of the pot black.
proverbs.meaning: Criticizing someone hypocritically for a fault you possess yourself.

proverbs.text: Nevah laugh when yoh bruddah get wet.
proverbs.translation: Never laugh when your brother gets rained on.
proverbs.meaning: Do not mock someone else's misfortune.

proverbs.text: Nonsense man use fork feh eat soup.
proverbs.translation: A foolish man uses a fork to eat soup.
proverbs.meaning: Fools always choose the hardest or most illogical way to do a simple task.

proverbs.translation: Nothing stays hidden forever.
proverbs.meaning: Secrets eventually come out into the light.

proverbs.translation: A rat trap never sleeps.
proverbs.meaning: Danger is constant and always lurking; stay alert.
Covetous, greedy, or envious behavior (calque, compare Twi).
Constant gossiping or blabbering (reduplication).

proverbs.translation: Take one's feet in one's hand.
proverbs.meaning: Run away as fast as possible to escape danger.

proverbs.translation: He who doesn't listen will feel.
proverbs.meaning: Those who ignore good advice or warnings will suffer the painful consequences.

proverbs.translation: Oh good!
proverbs.meaning: Serves you right! (Expressing satisfaction at someone's self-inflicted bad luck).
Personable address / 1st person singular address.

proverbs.translation: All right.
proverbs.meaning: Standard polite greeting exchanged when passing someone.

proverbs.translation: As one man to another.
proverbs.meaning: "I agree completely!", "Without a doubt!", or expression of solidarity/surprise.

proverbs.translation: All of you can lie!
proverbs.meaning: You've got to be kidding! / You're joking!

proverbs.translation: All of your ears are long.
proverbs.meaning: You all are being extremely nosy.

proverbs.translation: Big man / Boss man.
proverbs.meaning: Term of respect when addressing an esteemed male.

proverbs.translation: Cheese and bread!
proverbs.meaning: Goodness gracious! / Exclamation of shock or frustration.

proverbs.translation: Is that you?
proverbs.meaning: Warm exclamation when running into a friend after a long time.

proverbs.translation: That is a thing!
proverbs.meaning: Isn't that something! / How surprising!

proverbs.translation: The man!
proverbs.meaning: Hey! / Common interjection of surprise or annoyance.

proverbs.translation: Eh eh.
proverbs.meaning: Exclamation of surprise or disbelief (compare Twi ei eei).

proverbs.text: Happy as a fly under a dry cow tail, me son!
proverbs.translation: Happy as a fly under a dry cow's tail.
proverbs.meaning: Feeling extremely comfortable and content.

proverbs.translation: How do you mean?
proverbs.meaning: Rhetorical agreement: "Of course!", "You know it!".
Goodbye / I am leaving.

proverbs.translation: I am telling you!
proverbs.meaning: Believe me! / Absolute truth.

proverbs.text: I was born at night, but not last night!
proverbs.meaning: You can't fool me!
Rhetorical question: "You don't control me!"
Cool, peaceful, good vibes (Rastafarian).

proverbs.translation: Look here!
proverbs.meaning: Exclamation to draw someone's direct attention ("Look-kyea, see wha' happen deh!").
Traditional Crucian New Year greeting spoken in January.
Signature Crucian interjection used for emphasis or surprise.
Standard humble, friendly response when asked how you are doing.

Sweet talk, charm, or flirtatious speech (calque, compare Twi).
